clinicalPearls: Typically bilateral and multicystic, arising from marked luteinisation of the ovaries driven by beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin
Strongly associated with high or sustained beta-hCG levels, as seen in gestational trophoblastic disease, molar pregnancy, and multiple pregnancy
Also occurs in ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome following ovulation induction, where exogenous stimulation and hCG drive cyst formation
Often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, though the enlarged ovaries may cause a dragging pelvic discomfort or pressure symptoms
The ovaries commonly show a multilocular, spoke-wheel appearance on ultrasound with numerous thin-walled cysts
The cysts characteristically regress spontaneously once the beta-hCG level falls, so expectant management is usually appropriate
Complications include torsion, haemorrhage, or rupture of the enlarged ovaries, which may require intervention
reference.pathophysiology: Excessive circulating beta-hCG, or heightened ovarian sensitivity to normal levels, over-stimulates the theca interna cells lining the ovarian follicles. This drives exaggerated luteinisation and the formation of multiple fluid-filled cysts, usually affecting both ovaries and producing considerable ovarian enlargement. Because the process is hormonally driven, the cysts involute as the beta-hCG concentration declines, for example after evacuation of a molar pregnancy or delivery.
additionalDifferentials: Ovarian malignancy with bilateral cystic involvement
Bilateral functional cysts from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Serum beta-hCG to confirm and quantify the hormonal driver
Transvaginal or transabdominal ultrasound showing bilateral multilocular cysts
Pelvic ultrasound of the uterus to exclude a molar pregnancy or confirm a multiple pregnancy
Thyroid function tests, given the potential thyrotropic effect of very high hCG
Full blood count and observation for features of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
redFlags: Ovarian torsion presenting with acute severe pelvic pain
Haemorrhage or rupture of an enlarged ovary
Evidence of gestational trophoblastic disease requiring specialist management
Severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with tense ascites, breathlessness, or thromboembolic risk
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent, as theca lutein cysts almost always resolve spontaneously once the underlying hCG stimulus subsides, without the need for surgery.
pitfalls: Performing unnecessary surgery on cysts that would resolve spontaneously
Failing to identify an underlying molar pregnancy or gestational trophoblastic disease
Overlooking evolving ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome in an assisted-conception setting
Missing torsion or haemorrhage in a woman with markedly enlarged ovaries
management: Expectant, conservative management is the mainstay, as the cysts involute spontaneously once the beta-hCG stimulus falls
Treat the underlying driver — evacuation of a hydatidiform mole, delivery, or chemotherapy for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
Manage associated ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome supportively where that is the cause
Monitor with serial beta-hCG and pelvic ultrasound to confirm regression and exclude trophoblastic disease
Check thyroid function given the weak thyrotropic effect of very high hCG
Reserve surgery for acute complications such as torsion, rupture or haemorrhage, conserving ovarian tissue wherever possible
